summary.value: This paper presents a contrastive decoding approach tailored to radiology report generation (RRG) called. clinical contrastive decoding (CCD). The CCD framework adjusts the token logits of a pretrained multimodal large language model (MLLM) using the outputs of a pretrained image classifier, enabling a training-free method to enhance the generations of the MLLM. The authors additionally conduct an analysis on a potential source of hallucination in the generations of the MLLM within the context of RRG.

strengths.value:
●	 Interesting idea to understand the potential to utilize a pretrained classifier to enhance model generation without retraining the LLM. Interesting approach to modify the token logits backed by context provided evidence of a domain “expert” image model.

●	 Valuable analysis to try to quantify the impact of potentially misleading information in the model prompt. Empirical results do demonstrate differences, though perhaps still an open question as to why those differences exist.

●	 The manuscript is well prepared with generally clear writing, equations, figures, and tables.

weaknesses.value:
●	The authors’ claim on the impracticality of retrieval doesn’t seem well founded, it’s  poorly cited and in reality, computing similarities over precomputed embeddings of images or text should be relatively cheap compared to the LLM inference that the system needs to do anyways.

●	While section 3 and table 1 provide interesting empirical evidence that the generations are sensitive to the prompts, the conclusions stated by the authors are more conjecture than evidence-based claims. For example, lines 216-217 claim clinical terminology and standardized phrasing is more prevalent in the history or technique sections, yet it is easy to observe similar standardized clinical phrasing in the other note sections exemplified in figure 1a. Additionally, in the paragraph on lines 222-231, the authors claim certain findings are more prevalent in different note sections. The authors fail to discuss the general increase in performance for cardiomegaly, consolidation, and edema when including all note sections in the prompt. Further the claims that are made by the authors, in terms of why atelectasis and pleural effusion do worse, should be quantified rather than relying on citing a review article from 1996 that only reviews atelectasis. It would seem that there is a lack of clinical background and context for the authors to make broad claims about clinical practice.

●	It is confusing how the CCD framework is using the expert model predicted probabilities in the ECD arm of the method. Equation 5 shows the clipped bias for a single $\tilde{l}_i$ being “uniformly added to the token logits”; how is the symptom label “selected” (line 337)? Does the label change depending on the step t? Figure 2 seems to present the use of all labels for every step t, so it seems further clarification on this fundamental component of the method is warranted.

●	Relatedly, given the use of the 14 CheXpert labels as the grounding source of information, why should CCD mitigate hallucinations such as the example “AP and lateral” vs “single frontal” provided in Figure 1a or help the model determine the type of atelectasis in Figure 1b? It is additionally unclear based on the presented results and methodology whether the authors actually evaluated whether CCD could mitigate these hallucinations in the context of the varying prompt information. See related question below on table 2 vs table 1 results.

●	The presentation of relative change in performance overstates results and should be tempered. The absolute change in F1RadGraph is ~2.8%. Additionally, while this work aims to demonstrate the relative gain of CCD over its baseline model, it would still be beneficial to understand the magnitude of the gain relative to the more complex approaches the authors aim to beat. Some of these results are presented in Appendix Table 6, however these results demonstrate much weaker results for generalizability of CCD.

questions.value:
●	In your experiments in section 3 on prompt-induced hallucination, was the type of clinical context provided in the prompt? I.e. was the note section header given as part of the clinical context? This would help the model better understand the information it was given, otherwise the results of section 3 may be confounded by the lack of contextualization.

●	Figure 2 seems to show the CheXpert labels are single tokens, is that the case? I would suspect not, given then the need to retrain the tokenizer and model, perhaps this should be clarified.

●	Lines 344-345 mention the use of different decoding components in the logits processor, yet line 378/9 state the use of greedy decoding. This should be clarified as the decoding strategies used in the logits processor are not the same as the final decoding approach, yet it still has an impact on the output logits.

●	It is unclear if the radiology report generation results presented in Table 2 includes any of the context prompts that were assayed in Table 1. It would be a stronger result to understand how CCD has mitigated those hallucinations in the presence of potentially counterfactual information.

Thank you for your valuable suggestion and for your service in reviewing our paper. Our detailed responses to your comments are provided as follows:

***

# W1: Retrieval

Thank you for raising this point.

> ***"The authors' claim on the impracticality of retrieval doesn't seem well founded ... should be relatively cheap compared to the LLM inference that the system needs to do anyways."***

We would also like to clarify that the **additional cost referred to in our response is not related to computational efficiency**. As stated in Line 125, "...strict privacy regulations exacerbate the scarcity and imbalance of clinical training data..." and Line 141/142 further notes that such approaches "...raise privacy or security concerns..." and "...in out-of-distribution settings or when adapting to new benchmarks." Recent concurrent work [1] has also expressed similar views. Therefore, **the motivation of this work is not centred on reducing computational cost.** 

Moreover, Line 985 explicitly states: "Our focus is on test-time decoding. Therefore, we do not compare with ... or retrieval-based augmentation..." Consequently, discussions involving non-testing-time methods, such as additional data collection, external retrieval, or privacy-sensitive pipelines, lie outside the scope of this study. Even if retrieval-based methods are computationally inexpensive, they nevertheless fall outside the model decoding strategy that our work focuses on.

[1] Kim et al., "Rethinking Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Medicine: A Large-Scale, Systematic Expert Evaluation and Practical Insights" 2025-Nov

***

# W2: Clinical Background

Thank you for this meaningful suggestion.

> ***"While section 3 and table 1 provide interesting empirical evidence that the generations are sensitive to the prompts, the conclusions stated by the authors are more conjecture than evidence-based claims."***

We acknowledge that **our conclusions are based primarily on quantitative experiments** and do not include qualitative analyses such as radiologist assessments. As stated in Section 3 (Line 161), "we conduct empirical analyses to...prompt-induced medical hallucinations," and Section 3 is designed to validate this specific category of hallucinations. Our analysis is further scoped to the RRG task, as noted in Line 182: "we focus on the chest X-ray modality and the RRG task."

As noted in Line 201, "We follow prior work and adopt a set of lexical and radiology-specific metrics..." Consistent with previous studies, this represents **the standard empirical evaluation practice in this domain**. Methods such as LLaVA-Rad [2] and RADAR [3], as well as recent evaluations from Google [4], also rely on report-level scores for assessing radiology report generation task.

[2] Zambrano Chaves et al., "A clinically accessible small multimodal radiology model and evaluation metric for chest X-ray findings" Nature Communications 2025

[3] Hou et al., "RADAR: Enhancing Radiology Report Generation with Supplementary Knowledge Injection" ACL 2025

[4] Google, "MedGemma Technical Report" 2025

> ***"It would seem that there is a lack of clinical background and context for the authors to make broad claims about clinical practice."***

We acknowledge that **we are not clinically trained experts, which further underscores the importance of professional radiologist assessment**. In Appendix G (Line 1477: "...more robust validation would benefit from reader studies..."), we explicitly recognise this limitation and note that human evaluation would indeed strengthen the validation. However, **such studies are prohibitively expensive, and we are currently unable to support them.** We intend to incorporate expert reader studies in future work to further evaluate our method, and we will actively seek the necessary funding and opportunities to enable such assessments.

***

# W3: CCD Framework

We would like to clarify this point further.

> ***"...how is the symptom label 'selected' (line 337)?"***

**We select symptom labels directly from the expert model's default output.** As mentioned in Line 292, "These expert-provided symptom labels are filtered using a default threshold (e.g., $s_i > 0.5$), and the selected labels are...". This threshold corresponds to the recommended configuration used by the underlying symptom classifier.

## (following above)

> ***"Does the label change depending on the step `t`?"***

**The labels do not change with the decoding step `t`**. As noted in Section 4.1 (Line 289), "we use a DenseNet-based classifier ... given v " where `v` is the image. Line 291 further states that "from this expert model, we extract a set of clinical labels...". Therefore, **for a single chest X-ray, the labels obtained from the expert model are fixed from the outset**.

In contrast, `t` is introduced only in the context of language model decoding. As described in Line 269 ("Preliminaries of MLLM Generation") and Line 277 ("..the output logits at decoding step t are denoted as...”), the variable `t` refers exclusively to the autoregressive decoding steps of the LLM, not to the expert classifier.

> ***"Figure 2 seems to present the use of all labels for every step `t`,..."***

**Yes**, the initial expert-provided labels influence all subsequent decoding steps `t`. As illustrated in Figure 2, because the MLLM is an autoregressive model that generates text token by token, we must apply the guidance at every decoding step. This is why the notation `t` is introduced only after the model begins producing output tokens. **The left side of Figure 2 marks the "log-softmax" operation**, which indicates that `t `governs the propagation of logits through each decoding step. Representing the process in this way is therefore a more accurate and consistent formulation.

***

# W4: Mitigate Hallucination

We would like to clarify this point further.

> ***"Why should CCD mitigate hallucinations such as the example 'AP and lateral' vs 'single frontal' provided in Figure 1a "***

We **do not use these clinical sections** (e.g., Figure 1a, Line 58: "Portable anteroposterior (AP) and lateral chest radiograph") **as part of the model input**, thereby avoiding the ambiguity they introduce. Without these misleading sections, the model is able to produce the correct output such as 'single frontal'.

As noted in Section 3, Line 85, "prompt-induced medical hallucinations, triggered by clinically implausible or ambiguous prompts..", arise from the clinical sections contained in the dataset itself. Examples such as 'AP and lateral' originate from these raw report sections and can mislead the model at input. **The most direct way to eliminate such prompt-induced hallucinations is therefore simply not to use these clinical sections as part of the model input.** Accordingly, as illustrated in Figure 1a, our default prompt is used without any clinical context. **The only message the model receives is**: "Provide a detailed description of the findings in the radiology image."

> ***"why help the model determine the type of atelectasis in Figure 1b?"***

As noted in Line 291, "the selected labels are then used to construct a concise anchor prompt (e.g., ‘Attention to the following clinical instructions: Atelectasis, Cardiomegaly...’)." Therefore, if a chest X-ray contains a finding such as atelectasis, the expert model could provide a corresponding signal. 

**The example in Figure 1(b) illustrates this effect:** `"What type is the atelectasis? Attention to the following clinical instructions: Atelectasis."` In addition to this anchor prompt, the second-stage probability signals further reinforce the guidance (Section 4.2). Together, these signals help the model focus on the relevant pathology and support its downstream reasoning.

> ***"See related question below on table 2 vs table 1 results."***

***Please refer to the response to Question 4 below.***

***

# W5: Performance

Thank you for this constructive suggestion.

> ***"The presentation of relative change in performance overstates results and should be tempered. The absolute change in F1RadGraph is ~2.8%."***

We fully agree with your observation. Accordingly, **both the Abstract and Table 2 have been updated to report absolute rather than relative improvements.**

> ***"It would still be beneficial to understand the magnitude of the gain relative to the more complex approaches the authors aim to beat."***

We agree with this point. The strategies **we compare against are methods developed for the general domain**, and as shown in our experiments, several of them even reduce baseline performance when applied to radiology MLLMs. To the best of our knowledge, **at the time of submission, no prior work had proposed decoding strategies specifically designed to optimise radiology MLLMs**, and therefore no domain-specialised baselines were available for comparison.

As noted in Line 154, "While effective in such domains, these methods struggle to mitigate medical hallucinations in radiology..." Furthermore, Appendix D.1 (Line 1157 "The following is a brief overview of these methods.") provides an overview and discussion of each competing method, highlighting **why general-domain decoding approaches are not directly effective in this clinical setting.**

> ***"Some of these results are presented in Appendix Table 6, however these results demonstrate much weaker results for generalizability of CCD."***

We acknowledge that **CCD exhibits some limitations in generalisation**. This arises because **the default hyperparameters used for CCD were selected based on empirical optimisation** for MAIRA-2 on the RRG task, and therefore may not be optimal for other models.

As stated in Section 5.3 (Line 471), "the best empirical RadGraph-F1 score is achieved when both guidance strengths reach 0.5," and the ablation studies in Appendix E (Tables 7, 8, and 9) support this choice. Based on these observations, we adopt $\alpha = 0.5$ and $\beta = 0.5$ as the hyperparameter configuration for MAIRA-2. **Selecting hyperparameters through empirical validation is also a common practice for decoding strategies in the general domain**, and our choice aligns with prior work, such as VTI [5], in their hyperparameter design.

In addition, we have already acknowledged this limitation in generalisation, consistent with the statement in Line 1280: "This suggests that choosing appropriate hyperparameters for each model is critical to achieving a balanced trade-off between lexical and clinical performance." **We have included further discussion of this point in Appendix G.**

[5] Liu et al., "Reducing Hallucinations in Vision-Language Models via Latent Space Steering" ICLR Spotlight 2025

***

# Q1: Experiments

> ***"In your experiments in section 3 on prompt-induced hallucination, was the type of clinical context provided in the prompt? "***

Yes, we have ensured that the experimental design remains rigorous, and **we will include all original information accordingly**. As illustrated in Figure 1, Line 62 specifies the default template: "Provide a detailed description of the findings in the radiology image. Following clinical context: <clinical section>" When a clinical section is present, the prompt includes all content shown in the top-right of Figure 1, as indicated in Line 54 ("Clinical Section"). Thus, the full prompt in such cases becomes:
`"Provide a detailed description of the findings in the radiology image. Following clinical context: INDICATION:...TECHNIQUE:...COMPARISON:... HISTORY:..."`

This accurately reflects the raw clinical sections used in the dataset and ensures that our experimental setup faithfully represents the original input conditions.

***

# Q2: CheXpert Label

> ***"Figure 2 seems to show the CheXpert labels are single tokens, is that the case? I would suspect not..."***

Yes, you are correct — **they are simply abbreviations**. The abbreviations shown in the lower-left of Figure 2 are merely shorthand **name of the symptoms**, used for visual clarity and to avoid repeated long text in the figure. As stated in Line 291, "each $\ell_i$ denotes a finding (e.g., ‘Atelectasis’)", and Line 293 further clarifies that the anchor prompt is constructed as "Attention to the following clinical instructions: Atelectasis, Cardiomegaly...". Since these are standard free-text terms, the **LLM's tokenizer can recognise them without requiring any retraining.**

#  Q3: Logits Processor

Thank you for this meaningful question.

> ***"Lines 344-345 mention the use of different decoding components in the logits processor, yet line 378/9 state the use of greedy decoding."***

You are correct. **All our experiments employ greedy decoding**. We control this behaviour through the `LogitsProcessor()`, which governs decoding behaviour, sequence length, and related settings — **including greedy decoding**. This module is therefore an essential part of the generation framework and naturally incorporates the decoding strategy used in our experiments. **We have reiterated this point at Line 344 in the revised manuscript to improve clarity.**

***

# Q4: Context Prompt

Thank you for raising this question.

> ***"It is unclear if the radiology report generation results presented in Table 2 includes any of the context prompts that were assayed in Table 1."***

**For Table 1**, as stated in Line 198, "We adopt the default prompt shown in Figure 1(a) and use greedy decoding, the standard setting for radiology MLLMs. In each case, we append a different clinical section." Accordingly, **Table 1** compares the **default prompt with versions** that include the corresponding **clinical sections.** (e.g., `"Provide a detailed description of the findings in the radiology image. Following clinical context: INDICATION:...TECHNIQUE:...COMPARISON:... HISTORY:..."`)

**For Table 2**, Line 273 states: "For the default prompt, we represent it as x...". Thus, **Table 2** evaluates the model using **only the default prompt** and does **not** include any additional clinical sections. (e.g., `"Provide a detailed description of the findings in the radiology image."`)

summary.value: The paper proposes Clinical Contrastive Decoding (CCD), a training-free, retrieval-free inference method to reduce medical hallucinations in radiology MLLMs. CCD plugs in a task-specific expert classifier (e.g., CheXpert-style DenseNet) and uses its predicted labels and probabilities to (1) inject a “clinical anchor” into the prompt (SCD) and (2) bias token logits with calibrated logit offsets (ECD). Evaluated on MIMIC-CXR, IU-Xray, and CheXpert Plus across RRG and CXR-VQA, CCD improves several clinical metrics (e.g., up to +17% RadGraph-F1 on MIMIC-CXR) without retraining the base MLLM.

strengths.value:
1. The paper is well-motivated. Instead of just proposing a new method, the authors first dedicate Section 3 to diagnosing a specific, tangible problem: MLLMs "overreact to clinical context" , and the clinical sections in reports "are not always reliable sources of guidance". This empirical analysis provides a strong justification for their solution.
2. The proposed CCD framework is both training-free and retrieval-free. This is a significant advantage in the medical domain, as it avoids the cost, privacy concerns, and complexity associated with retraining models or maintaining large retrieval databases.

weaknesses.value:
1. The empirical motivation in Table 1, while interesting, is not as compelling as it could be. The authors demonstrate that adding noisy or counterfactual context (like "comparison" or "technique" sections) degrades performance. This is somewhat expected, as the model is not given the prior images needed for comparison, confusing its generation task.
A stronger motivation for CCD would be to complete this analysis by showing the opposite:
First, demonstrate that feeding the model clean, structured labels (like those from an expert classifier) as prompt context actually improves performance over the baseline in Table 1.
Then, contrast this with the performance degradation when using the noisy, original report sections.

This would more forcefully prove the central hypothesis: MLLMs are harmed by bad context but benefit from good context, thereby providing a stronger justification for the CCD framework.

2. The framework's performance is fundamentally coupled to the quality and design of the expert model, which introduces several limitations:
a. The framework's effectiveness is capped by the expert model's accuracy. As the authors' own ablations suggest, a stronger expert yields better results. Conversely, a weak or systematically biased expert model could, in principle, steer the MLLM to replicate its own errors, potentially propagating biases.

b.  The use of a simple > 0.5 probability threshold to select expert labels for the anchor prompt is suboptimal, especially for highly imbalanced medical datasets where clinically important findings are often rare. More sophisticated, data-driven thresholding techniques (e.g., maximizing F1-score) would be better suited to calibrate the expert guidance.
[1] The limits of fair medical imaging AI in real-world generalization. Nature Medicine.
[2] Algorithmic encoding of protected characteristics in chest X-ray disease detection models. Lancet

c. The CheXpert ontology’s 14 pathologies provide limited morphological and positional detail (e.g., scarring, lesion location), which explains the observed performance dips in VQA categories like Location and Type.
This reflects an inherent ceiling for CCD’s guidance. The authors could extend their framework by incorporating expert findings for anatomical regions and observation types (using RADGRAPH), inspired by:
[1] Anatomy-Guided Weakly-Supervised Abnormality Localization in Chest X-rays. MICCAI 2022
[2] Dividing and Conquering a BlackBox to a Mixture of Interpretable Models: Route, Interpret, Repeat. ICML 2023
[3] Distilling blackbox to interpretable models for efficient transfer learning. MICCAI 2023

3. The evaluation could be expanded to include LLM-as-a-Judge metrics, particularly the recently proposed GREEN framework (EMNLP 2024, “Generative Radiology Report Evaluation and Error Notation”). Such metrics capture clinically nuanced correctness and could provide complementary insights beyond traditional lexical or structured metrics.

4. The paper positions itself as a solution to prompt-induced hallucinations, as identified in Table 1 where "comparison" sections cause errors. However, it is unclear how the proposed CCD framework—which guides the MLLM based on findings in the current image—would explicitly prevent the model from spontaneously hallucinating references to past exams. This common and problematic type of hallucination seems unaddressed by the current mechanism.


5. The paper currently lacks consistent figure references and variable definitions.
Figure 2 is cited as having panels (a) and (b), but no such markings are visible.
The variable c in line 298 is undefined; it appears to refer to the structured labels from the expert model, which should be explicitly stated.
Improving figure annotations and notational clarity will make the methodology easier to follow.

questions.value:
1. Since the framework’s success depends heavily on the expert classifier, how sensitive is CCD to expert calibration and label-imbalance effects?

2. Given that the 14 CheXpert labels lack morphological or positional coverage, do the authors plan to incorporate anatomical and observation-level findings (e.g., from RADGRAPH or anatomy-guided classifiers) as additional expert concepts?
How might CCD generalize to these richer ontologies, which could address the VQA “Location/Type” performance dips?

3. Have the authors considered evaluating with LLM-as-a-Judge metrics such as GREEN (EMNLP 2024)?

Thank you for your valuable expertise in this space and your service in reviewing our paper! Our detailed response to your concerns/questions is listed as follows:

***

# W1: Motivation

We acknowledge that this line of reasoning is indeed helpful for strengthening the paper. 

> ***"A stronger motivation for CCD would be to complete this analysis by showing the opposite: First, demonstrate that feeding the model clean, structured labels (like those from an expert classifier) as prompt context actually improves performance over the baseline in Table 1. Then, contrast this with the performance degradation when using the noisy, original report sections."***

Our current motivation is grounded in the observation introduced in Line 85, where we state that "...prompt-induced medical hallucinations, triggered by clinically implausible or ambiguous prompts..." These sections originate from the original reports, which motivates the ablation in Table 1 in Section 3.

**Regarding your suggestion to feed clean, structured labels from an expert classifier,** if we understand correctly, this refers to providing these labels directly to the model without applying any hyperparameter control.  **Within our framework, this corresponds to the special case of setting $\alpha = 1$ (instead of the default 0.5),** meaning that the model relies entirely on the expert-provided labels. In Appendix D.2, Table 7, when the MLLM fully depends on these expert labels ($\alpha = 1$,), performance improves on certain metrics. However, with the default setting of $\alpha = 0.5$, a broader range of clinically meaningful metrics, including RadGraph-F1, reaches its peak performance.


# W2: Performance Limitations

Thank you for your detailed and insightful comments.

> ***"a. The framework's effectiveness is capped by the expert model's accuracy ... Conversely, a weak or systematically biased expert model could, in principle, steer the MLLM to replicate its own errors, potentially propagating biases."***

We did take this into consideration and **conducted robustness tests to evaluate the effect of unreliable expert signals on the MLLM**. As shown in Appendix E.2, Line 1387 reports that "although the random setting introduces mild fluctuations in performance, there is no significant degradation across lexical or clinical metrics," consistent with the results in Table 10 (where 6 metrics increase and 4 show slight decreases compared with the baseline). Line 1390 further notes that "it enhances downstream performance only when the expert provides meaningful guidance, while gracefully falling back to the base model's behaviour otherwise." 


> ***"b: The use of a simple > 0.5 probability threshold to select expert labels for the anchor prompt is suboptimal..."***

We fully agree with your point, and we have taken this aspect into account. The "threshold" here refers to the final probability outputs of the expert model, **which already incorporate threshold-based normalisation**. As noted in Line 288, the DenseNet-based classifier applies symptom-specific thresholds and sigmoid normalisation during inference. These thresholds are implemented directly in the official TorchXRayVision [1] model, **where each symptom category is associated with its own calibrated threshold in the classifier's forward pass** (see the [official implementation line 343-357](https://github.com/mlmed/torchxrayvision/blob/df3c84c8c31bebbeb8696d400c862e615110bdfc/torchxrayvision/models.py#L343C1-L357C1) for details).

[1] Cohen et al, "TorchXRayVision: A library of chest X-ray datasets and models" 2021

> ***"c: The CheXpert ontology's 14 pathologies provide limited morphological and positional detail, which explains the observed performance dips in VQA categories like Location and Type. The authors could extend their framework by incorporating expert findings for anatomical regions and observation types (using RADGRAPH)"***

Thank you for this highly constructive suggestion. Our contribution primarily aims to show that **incorporating an expert model can enhance MLLM performance on downstream tasks**, rather than covering a broader set of label categories. For this study, we therefore use the 14-label CheXpert symptom-level classifier. **This choice remains flexible, and the module can be adapted to future expert models should more comprehensive label sets become available.** As stated in Line 287, "we focus on the 14 pathology labels defined in the CheXpert ontology..." Symptom-level signals are the only form of guidance that the expert model can provide within the scope of this study. 

**Regarding the slight drop in Location/Type about VQA**, we also highlight this in the caption of
Table 3.  In Appendix F, Figure 4 (Line 1421) further explains that in these examples, "model outputs that are vague or under-specified (i.e., partially correct but lacking clinical precision)" lead to a dip that is largely an artefact of the evaluation procedure rather than a genuine performance drop. Additionally, Appendix A provides a detailed discussion of our research aims (A.1) and research scope (A.2). As stated in Line 987, "Nor do we attempt to eliminate all forms of medical hallucination." Incorporating anatomical-region or observation-type signals therefore falls outside the scope of the present study.

**We agree that incorporating richer structural cues, such as RadGraph-based information, is an excellent direction.** This aligns well with our planned future work, and we would welcome the opportunity to collaborate in exploring this direction further if possible.

***

# W3: Evaluation

Thank you for raising this point.

> ***"The evaluation could be expanded to include LLM-as-a-Judge metrics, particularly the recently proposed GREEN framework..."***

We agree and have added a GREEN score to assess the improvement over the baseline. Due to page limitations, this analysis has been included in Appendix D.1.


|               | GREEN |
|----|----|
| MAIRA-2   | 18.03 |
| + CCD     | 19.14 |

For the original manuscript, Section 3 (Line 202) states that "We follow prior work and adopt a set of lexical and radiology-specific metrics...", which are the standard and cost-effective evaluation practices in this domain. **Our setup follows prior work such as MAIRA-2 [2], RADAR [3], and LLaVA-Rad [4], using the overlapping lexical and clinical metrics adopted in these studies to ensure broad and consistent coverage.**

Using more compute-intensive evaluation methods (e.g., GREEN or other LLM-based evaluators such as GPT-5) typically requires additional GPU resources or API costs. As mentioned in Line 1085, our experiments were conducted under limited computational capacity and inference-time constraints, using only two low-memory GPUs for all MLLM evaluation. **Requesting further GPU resources or significantly extending the computation time is currently beyond our affordable budget.**

[2] Bannur et al., "MAIRA-2: Grounded Radiology Report Generation" 2024

[3] Hou et al., "RADAR: Enhancing Radiology Report Generation with Supplementary Knowledge Injection" ACL 2025

[4] Zambrano Chaves et al., "A clinically accessible small multimodal radiology model and evaluation metric for chest X-ray findings" Nature Communications 2025

***

# W4: Framework

We would like to clarify this point further.

> ***"However, it is unclear how the proposed CCD framework—which guides the MLLM based on findings in the current image—would explicitly prevent the model from spontaneously hallucinating references to past exams."***

Our method **avoids prompt-induced hallucinations at the model input** by preventing any downstream influence from the noisy or misleading clinical sections present in the original reports. In other words, it does not use this metadata.

summary.value:
The paper introduces Clinical Contrastive Decoding (CCD), a training-free, retrieval-free, inference-time method to curb medical hallucinations in radiology multimodal LLMs. CCD plugs in a task-specific expert model (e.g., a CheXpert-style chest-x-ray classifier) and applies a two-stage, token-logit adjustment during decoding:

* Symptom-grounded Contrastive Decoding (SCD): adds expert-predicted labels as a concise “clinical anchor” prompt and blends anchor-conditioned logits with the base logits to reduce false negatives.

* Expert-informed Contrastive Decoding (ECD): converts expert probabilities into clipped logit biases (bounded by a likelihood-ratio cap) to suppress false positives.

strengths.value:
* CCD requires no retraining and only an external expert classifier, making it easy to add to existing radiology MLLMs while directly optimizing clinical fidelity at decode time.

* Improvements hold across datasets, metrics (RadGraph-F1, RaTE, Temporal-F1, CheXbert), and tasks (RRG, VQA), with clear ablations (remove SCD/ECD, vary α/β, swap experts) supporting the mechanism.

weaknesses.value:
* Guidance is limited by the 14 CheXpert labels; categories like Location/Type in VQA degrade slightly, suggesting missed morphology/topography signals and potential brittleness outside the expert’s ontology.  

* Core knobs (α, β, γ) are fixed across tasks/models; there’s no adaptive controller tied to uncertainty or prompt/model state, leaving performance-vs-fluency trade-offs hand-tuned. 

* While multi-metric, the paper reports limited variance/seed statistics, human evaluation, or calibration/uncertainty analysis; compute/latency overhead of running the expert online is only qualitatively discussed. 

* Experiments focus on CXR single-view RRG/VQA; generalization to CT/MRI/US, multi-series exams, or longitudinal/report-level reasoning is unproven.

questions.value:
* How would CCD scale beyond CheXpert-14—e.g., to morphology (size/shape), location, devices, lines/tubes, or temporal comparisons—without re-training the expert?

* How sensitive is CCD to expert miscalibration or domain shift (different scanners/hospitals, pediatric vs. adult)? Any safeguards (e.g., temperature scaling, conformal thresholds) to avoid propagating expert errors?

* What is the end-to-end overhead (ms/image, GPU memory) of running the expert and logit processors at decode time, and how does it compare to training-time mitigation (e.g., COMT/RAG-style methods)?

* Beyond automated metrics, have you performed radiologist blind reads or error-taxonomy audits to verify reductions in harmful hallucinations (e.g., false effusion/pneumothorax claims)?

# Q2: Sensitive & Expert Model

Thank you for raising this important question

> ***"How sensitive is CCD to expert miscalibration or domain shift(different scanners/hospitals..."***

**Our results indicate that CCD is not noticeably sensitive to label-imbalance effects**, as imbalanced expert signals do not lead to notable performance drops. We also evaluated CCD under unreliable or imbalanced expert signals.  As shown in Appendix E.2, Line 1387 reports that "although the random setting introduces mild fluctuations in performance, there is no significant degradation across lexical or clinical metrics," consistent with the results in Table 10 (where 6 metrics increase and 4 show slight decreases compared with the baseline).

**Regarding the limitation of domain shift**, this is consistent with the discussion provided in Appendix G. As noted in Line 1468, "both the MIMIC-CXR and Medical-CXR-VQA datasets originate from the same institution", and Line 1470 further notes that this "...introduce institution-specific biases in patient demographics...". In addition, Line 1488 highlights that "real-world clinical practice often involves lower-quality inputs, including portable X-rays or images from heterogeneous equipment". Therefore, **addressing this concern would require substantially broader and more diverse datasets, which is currently beyond our cost constraints and the scope of this study.**


> ***"Any safeguards to avoid propagating expert errors?"***

**Yes**, our method controls this behaviour through ***the choice of hyperparameters*** and the ***two‐stage contrastive decoding procedure***. Thus, the expert model serves only as an auxiliary guidance signal rather than a dominant component. 

For example, as noted in Line 329, "Inspired by clinical practice, where likelihood ratios ... cap the logit-based bias ...", we apply clipping to appropriately constrain the influence of the expert model, and the hyperparameters further regulate the strength of this guidance. **An interesting observation** is reported in Line 1390: "It enhances downstream performance only when the expert provides meaningful guidance, while gracefully falling back to the base model's behaviour otherwise."

***

# Q3: Overhead

> ***"What is the end-to-end overhead (ms/image, GPU memory) of running the expert and logit processors at decode time?"***

Our experiments were conducted on two NVIDIA RTX 3090 GPUs (24 GB each) with BF16 precision. On average, CCD introduces an end-to-end inference-time overhead of approximately 1.45× compared with standard greedy decoding. As noted in Appendix C, this overhead naturally varies across radiology MLLMs due to differences in model size and architecture.

> ***"how does it compare to training-time mitigation?"***

**We believe that such a comparison may not be entirely fair.** As stated in Line 985, "Our focus is on test-time decoding. Therefore, we do not compare with approaches that involve architectural modifications, additional training, or retrieval-based augmentation requiring external corpora."

Models that employ training strategies (e.g., MAIRA-1 [4]), data augmentation (e.g., LLaVA-Rad [5]), or even retrieval-based methods (e.g., RADAR [6]) **can still apply CCD as a decoding strategy after training**, as shown in Table 6. Appendix D.2 further provides a detailed discussion of how CCD integrates with different models. Therefore, comparing CCD with training-time mitigation methods is not conceptually appropriate and lies beyond the scope of our study.

***

# Q4: Human Evaluation

> ***"have you performed radiologist blind reads or error-taxonomy audits to verify reductions in harmful hallucinations"***

**We fully agree on the importance of human evaluation.** As noted in our response to **W3**, Appendix G (Line 1477) similarly acknowledges the value of radiologist-based assessment. **We hope to incorporate expert reader studies in the future to further validate the method, and we will actively seek the necessary funding and opportunities to support such evaluations.** For the present study, we therefore adopt the standard and cost-effective evaluation practices commonly used in this domain.

***

We sincerely hope that our responses have addressed your concerns. If we have left any notable points of concern overlooked, we would greatly appreciate your further feedback, and we will attend to them. Additionally, we will incorporate all the clarifications and improvements mentioned above in the final manuscript. Thanks again for your thoughtful review and consideration.
